title: Keeping the Heat Moving: How a Data Centre Stays Cool
performance: given a cooling alarm or a failed part in a data hall, the viewer can trace where the heat goes from server to outdoor air, name what each link does, and predict what happens next and what keeps the room running

audience.assumed_prior: knows computers get warm and data centres hold many servers; has never seen cooling plant
audience.why: mixed corporate audience including non-engineers, per the brief
audience.motivation: the services they depend on live in these rooms; a cooling incident is something they may hear about and want to understand calmly
audience.context: desktop at work, sound on, captions on

strategy.name: worked_example_led
strategy.rationale: one data hall followed from a single rack outward is the clearest way for non-engineers to see a chain of parts; each part is seen working before it is named
strategy.signature_move: follow the heat one step further out, show the part that carries it, THEN give the part its name

misconceptions.belief: air conditioning makes cold and destroys the heat
misconceptions.why_tempting: the air coming out feels cold, so it seems the machine produces cold

misconceptions.belief: if one cooling unit breaks, the servers overheat straight away
misconceptions.why_tempting: the cooling seems to be one machine, so losing part of it sounds like losing all of it

misconceptions.belief: blowing more cold air anywhere in the room is enough
misconceptions.why_tempting: more cold air sounds like more cooling

hook.sketch: A quiet data hall on a normal day; every server is turning its power into heat right now. Where does all of it go, and what if it stopped going?

arc.promise: by the end you can follow the heat out of the building and say what happens when one link fails
arc.bridge_from_prior: sec1 opens from the warm back of a laptop and a fridge that moves heat out of its box

sections.goal: the viewer can explain that servers turn their power into heat and that cooling moves heat rather than destroying it
the viewer can describe the air path from cold aisle through the server to the hot aisle and back to the CRAH
the viewer can describe what the pumps and the chiller do in the chilled water loop and where the heat leaves the building
the viewer can use the N+1 rule to predict what happens when one pump or CRAH fails
the viewer can explain what alarms and the water already in the loop do while a spare takes over, and what happens if cooling is not restored

arc.payoff: back to the quiet hall, now seen as a moving chain of heat from server to outdoor air, with a spare standing by at each link

practice_ladder.what: the heat followed link by link, each part shown working then named
a CRAH fails; the narrator shows the spare taking over and leaves the viewer to say why nothing overheated
a pump stops; the viewer predicts the next step before it is shown

recall_moments.prompt_sketch: Name the links in order, from the server to the outdoor air.
One pump in an N+1 loop stops. What happens next?
recall_moments.answer: the standby pump starts, usually automatically; the alarm tells operators to fix the failed one; the chilled water in the pipes buys a little time
recall_moments.tempting_wrong: the servers overheat at once: the spare and the water already in the loop keep the hall within range

transfer_tasks: the next time you hear of a cooling alarm in a data centre, ask which link failed and whether its spare took over

persona.voice: a calm colleague who knows the building and walks the viewer through it
persona.delivery_notes: unhurried on each new part, a beat of pause before naming it; even and reassuring in the failure section; brisk on the recap

gagne.attention: hook: the quiet hall and where its heat goes
gagne.objective: promise: follow the heat out and know what a failure means
gagne.recall_prior: sec1 bridge from a laptop and a fridge
gagne.present: sections follow the heat outward, in order
gagne.guidance: signature move: show the part, then name it
gagne.practice: recall prompt after sec3; quiz after sec5
gagne.feedback: quiz answer explained, including the tempting wrong reading
gagne.transfer: transfer task: ask which link failed and whether the spare took over

merrill.problem_centered: the one data hall and its heat is the running problem
merrill.demonstration: each link shown carrying heat before it is named
merrill.application: faded CRAH failure, then the pump check

mayer.coherence: one hall only; no efficiency metrics or cost
mayer.redundancy: screen shows the building and short labels; narration explains
mayer.contiguity: each part's label appears as it is named
mayer.segmenting: five short sections, one link or one idea each
mayer.pre_training: sec1 sets 'heat is moved' before any equipment is named

arcs.relevance: the services they use live in these rooms
arcs.satisfaction: the viewer predicts the pump failure correctly
